## Techniques

Source: https://openlabs.duckurity.com/technique

Vulnerability classes, defined once. Each technique links every lab that exercises it.
Start with [broken object-level authorization](/technique/idor). See also [authentication bypass](/technique/auth-bypass), [SSRF](/technique/ssrf), and [command injection](/technique/command-injection). Browse all [labs](/labs) when it is solved.

## API version enumeration

Source: https://openlabs.duckurity.com/technique/api-version-enumeration

## Overview
API version enumeration is the process of finding and comparing the versions of an API that an application still exposes. A version in a path, hostname, header, or media type is not a vulnerability by itself. The security issue appears when an older surface remains reachable with weaker authorization, validation, rate limits, logging, or business rules.
This is an inventory problem before it is an exploitation problem. Teams often document the current version while a legacy deployment remains live for an old mobile app, a partner integration, or a forgotten internal client. OWASP describes this wider failure as [improper inventory management](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa9-improper-inventory-management/).
> **A version is a separate security surface**
>
> Do not assume that a check fixed in one version exists in every version. Compare behaviour with the same authenticated context and request intent.
## How APIs expose versions
The version number is not always a path segment. Record the complete request shape before concluding that a version does not exist.
| Location | Production-style form |
| --- | --- |
| Path | `/api/v2/orders` |
| Hostname | `v1.api.example.test/orders` |
| Header | `API-Version: 2024-06-01` |
| Media type | `Accept: application/vnd.example.v1+json` |
| Query parameter | `/orders?api-version=2024-06-01` |
| Deployment name | `https://legacy.example.test/api/orders` |
Versions can also be implied by client bundles, OpenAPI documents, SDK package names, deprecation headers, changelogs, browser network traffic, and error messages. These are discovery clues. Confirm them through the permitted lab interface.
## Examples
### A legacy endpoint has a weaker ownership check
Consider a project-management service. Its current API checks that a user belongs to the project before returning an export. An older endpoint still accepts the same object reference but looks it up globally after authentication. The version is not the flaw. The missing object-level authorization in the older handler is the flaw.
This pattern is common when two services, middleware stacks, or codebases own different versions. A fix added to the current service does not automatically protect a legacy service.
### A retired operation remains published
A payment provider removes a bulk update operation from its new API documentation. The old operation still answers requests because an API gateway route was never disabled. It may lack newer schema validation, auditing, or per-field authorization. The lesson is to compare the complete route and its controls, not only the version label.
### Version selection falls back silently
Some APIs select a version through an `Accept` or custom header. A proxy, SDK, or client bug can drop that header and route a request to a default version. If the default is older and less protected, the fallback becomes part of the security boundary. Capture response headers and content types as well as the response body.
## A methodical approach in an authorized lab
Begin with the documented or visible API. Use it as the baseline for route names, methods, authentication, and expected schemas.
1. Identify every visible version marker in routes, hosts, headers, media types, and documentation.
2. Build a small version matrix. Keep the method, session, body, and object reference constant for each comparison.
3. Test only plausible versions and naming patterns supported by the lab evidence.
4. Record status codes, response headers, fields, schemas, and authorization behaviour for each response.
5. Treat `401`, `403`, `405`, redirects, and distinct error messages as useful inventory signals. They can prove that a route exists even when access is denied.
6. Compare controls, not only content. Note differences in ownership checks, validation, pagination, rate limits, and error handling.
Keep the matrix small and explainable. Broad unbounded scans add noise and can miss version forms that use headers or hostnames. A reproducible request set is more valuable than a long list of guesses.
## How to compare responses
Use a consistent table in your notes:
| Version selector | Route and method | Authentication result | Schema or policy difference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Current baseline | `GET /api/...` | Expected result | Current control observed |
| Candidate legacy version | Same intent | Denied, accepted, or different | Difference to investigate |
Do not treat a `404` as conclusive. A gateway may rewrite errors, hide a route, or require a different version selector. A `405 Method Not Allowed` can be strong evidence that a path is real but the method is wrong. A response with a different content type or deprecation header can also identify a distinct handler.
## Common mistakes
### Assuming `v1`, `v2`, and `v3` are the only shapes
Many APIs use dates, vendor media types, dedicated hosts, or unversioned legacy paths. Follow the application's own naming evidence.
### Calling every old version vulnerable
A deprecated endpoint can be secure. Report a concrete security regression such as a missing authorization check, an exposed operation, or weaker input validation. "An older version responds" is useful inventory information, not a complete vulnerability finding.
### Comparing different requests
If the method, body, object reference, or session changes between tests, the result is ambiguous. Hold them steady while changing the version selector.
### Forgetting non-production surfaces
Staging, beta, partner, mobile, and legacy hosts may use different authentication and deployment policies. They matter only when they are in your authorized scope.
## How developers prevent it
Maintain an inventory of all hosts, versions, routes, owners, and data classifications. Retire old routes at the gateway and application layers. Apply shared authentication, authorization, validation, logging, and rate-limit controls across every surviving version.
- Publish an accurate deprecation and retirement schedule.
- Remove unused routes instead of merely hiding them from documentation.
- Test old and current versions with the same authorization test suite.
- Reject unsupported version selectors predictably.
- Monitor traffic to deprecated versions before removal.
- Include gateways, serverless functions, partner APIs, and mobile backends in the inventory.
## Related labs
Apply this technique after studying it:
- [Firmdrama](/labs/firmdrama)
Browse all [labs](/labs), then read [how to play](/play) before starting a lab.
## FAQ
### Is API version enumeration the same as finding a shadow API?
It is one way to find an undocumented or poorly inventoried surface. A shadow API can also be an unversioned service, a forgotten host, or an internal endpoint exposed by mistake.
### Does a 404 prove that a version does not exist?
No. The version may use a header, a hostname, a date format, or a gateway that intentionally hides route details. Use the application's evidence and compare request shapes.
### What makes an old version a security finding?
A demonstrated difference that weakens security, such as a missing authorization check, an exposed retired operation, or absent input validation. Version age alone is not enough.
### What should a writeup include?
Include the baseline request, the exact version selector, the controlled comparison, the observed policy difference, and the affected authorization boundary.

## Authentication bypass

Source: https://openlabs.duckurity.com/technique/auth-bypass

## Overview
Authentication bypass happens when a login or session check accepts something other than a genuine, verified credential — a field the client controls, a comparison that isn't actually enforced, or a code path that skips verification under specific input.
## Examples
Watch for login flows that echo back or accept unexpected fields, GraphQL mutations with more arguments than the UI sends, or endpoints that behave differently when a field is omitted versus empty. Test with malformed, missing, or unexpected input types.
## Related labs
Practise on a live target:
- [TechVault](/labs/techvault) — a GraphQL login that doesn't verify what it should.
Browse all [labs](/labs) when it is solved.
## FAQ
**Is this the same as broken access control?**
No. Access control (like IDOR) is about authorization after you're already authenticated. Auth bypass is about getting authenticated (or treated as authenticated) without a valid credential.
**Do I need special tooling?**
A GraphQL client or `curl` is enough. Read [how to play](/play) for the loop.

## Client-side authorization decisions

Source: https://openlabs.duckurity.com/technique/client-side-authorization-decisions

## Overview
A client-side authorization decision is any check that decides whether an action is allowed, running entirely in code the user's own device executes, with the result trusted without independent server-side verification. Common shapes: a transfer-limit check in app code before calling an API, a feature flag read from local state, a role check in JavaScript before showing or hiding a button, or a licence check performed entirely on-device.
The client is attacker-controlled hardware running attacker-reachable code. Any decision made there can be observed, patched, or skipped by someone with the right access to that device or app process. This is not a mobile-specific or Frida-specific issue; it is the same failure whether the client is a native app, a browser, or a desktop binary. What changes by platform is how easy the client is to inspect and alter.
> **Authentication proves identity. It does not relocate authorization.**
>
> A client that correctly identifies its user has told the server who is asking. Whether that user may perform the requested action is a decision the server must still make, using its own state, every time.
## Examples
### A limit enforced only on-device
```kotlin
// TransferViewModel.kt
fun onConfirmTransfer(amount: Long) {
    if (amount > wallet.maxTransferLimit) {
        showError("Amount exceeds your limit")
        return
    }
    api.submitTransfer(amount) // server trusts the amount it receives
}
```
If the server endpoint behind `submitTransfer` accepts any amount the client sends and only the app's own `if` statement enforces the limit, patching that check (or calling the endpoint directly, bypassing the app's UI entirely) removes the limit completely. The server received a number; it never independently decided whether that number was allowed.
### A role flag trusted from local state
```javascript
// Trusting a client-stored flag instead of a server-verified session claim.
if (localStorage.getItem('role') === 'admin') {
    renderAdminPanel();
    callAdminApi(); // the API must still check the caller's real role server-side
}
```
Hiding a button is a UI convenience. If `callAdminApi()` does not independently verify the caller's role on the server, setting `localStorage.role = 'admin'` is sufficient to reach it.
### A check defeated by patched logic, not patched data
In a compiled app, the equivalent of editing `localStorage` is hooking or patching the method that performs the check, so it always returns the permissive branch. The data sent to the server can look entirely legitimate; only the decision that produced it was tampered with.
## How to recognise it in an authorized lab
1. Identify every action that has a value threshold, role, or entitlement gating it (a limit, an admin feature, a paywalled capability).
2. Trace where the gating decision is made: client code only, or client code followed by an independent server-side check using its own state.
3. If only the client decides, attempt to reach the server-side effect while skipping or altering the client-side decision: call the API directly, patch the client's check with a hook, or modify the value the client was about to send after its check already passed.
4. Confirm the server performs the privileged action anyway. That confirms the authorization decision lived entirely client-side.
5. Distinguish this from input validation: a value out of range being silently clamped by the server is a different (and better) outcome than the server performing the action with the attacker-supplied value unchanged.
## Common mistakes and false assumptions
### "Obfuscation or anti-tampering makes the client check sufficient"
Obfuscation raises the cost of reading or patching client code. It does not change where the decision is made. A sufficiently motivated attacker, or a lab built to practice exactly this, still reaches the server endpoint with the check skipped.
### "The mobile app can't be scripted the way a browser can"
Instrumentation frameworks give an attached process the same reach into app logic that browser developer tools give into a web page's JavaScript. The platform differs; the trust boundary problem is identical.
### "We validate input types and lengths server-side, so we're covered"
Type and length validation is necessary but answers a different question than authorization. The server can correctly accept a well-formed request for an amount, a role, or an action that it should have rejected because the requester was not entitled to it.
## Impact
The impact scales with what the bypassed check was protecting: a transfer limit becomes unenforced, a paywalled feature becomes free, an admin action becomes available to any authenticated user, or in the most severe case, any user at all. Because the request the server receives can be well-formed, these bypasses often leave no obvious trace at the input-validation layer.
## How developers prevent it
- Re-verify every authorization-relevant decision server-side, using server-held state (the stored balance, the user's actual role from the database, the real entitlement), never a value or flag the client supplied.
- Treat client-side checks as UX only: they may prevent an honest user from submitting an invalid request, but they must never be the only gate on a privileged action.
- For mobile specifically, assume any on-device check can be read, hooked, or patched by someone with physical or instrumented access to the device, and design the server contract accordingly.
- Log and alert on server-side rejections of requests that an honest client should never have produced, since they are a strong signal of a bypassed client check.
## Related labs
Apply this technique after studying it:
- [Nexawallet](/labs/nexawallet)
Browse all [labs](/labs), then read [how to play](/play) before starting a lab.
## FAQ
### Is this the same as broken object-level authorization (IDOR)?
They are related failures in the same family. IDOR is about the server failing to check *which object* a request may touch. Client-side authorization is about the server failing to independently decide *whether an action is allowed at all*, having delegated that decision to the client.
### Does HTTPS prevent this?
No. Transport encryption protects the request in transit. It does nothing about whether the request itself should have been honoured once it arrives.
### Can rate limiting replace server-side authorization?
No. Rate limiting constrains how often a request can be made, not whether a given request was authorized. Both can be relevant; neither substitutes for the other.

## Command injection

Source: https://openlabs.duckurity.com/technique/command-injection

## Overview
Command injection happens when user-supplied input is concatenated into a string that's passed to a system shell, instead of being passed as a discrete, escaped argument. Shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `` ` ``, `$()`) let you append or chain additional commands.
## Examples
Watch for features that shell out to system tools: file conversion, network diagnostics (ping, traceroute-style tools), archive extraction. Try metacharacters in any field that ends up looking like a filename, hostname, or path.
## Related labs
Practise on a live target:
- [TechVault](/labs/techvault) — an internal service that builds a shell command from unsanitized input.
Browse all [labs](/labs) when it is solved.
## FAQ
**Is this the same as SQL injection?**
Same family of flaw — unsanitized input reaching an interpreter — but the interpreter here is the OS shell, not a database engine.
**Do I need special tooling?**
A browser or `curl` is enough to start. Read [how to play](/play) for the loop.

## Framework-level Frida hooking past ART inlining

Source: https://openlabs.duckurity.com/technique/frida-framework-level-hooking-past-art-inlining

## Overview
A Frida script that calls `Java.use('com.app.Checker').check.implementation = ...` assumes every call to `check()` passes through one callable method entry point. The Android Runtime (ART) does not guarantee that. When a method is small, final, or otherwise provably safe to inline, ART's ahead-of-time (AOT) compiler or JIT can inline its body directly into the caller. The call instruction disappears. A hook installed on the method's entry point never fires, because execution never reaches that entry point at runtime.
This is not an anti-Frida trick by itself. It is a standard compiler optimization that happens to defeat a hooking technique built on the assumption that a method call is a call.
## Examples
### The hook that never fires
```java
// Checker.java
final class Checker {
    static boolean isDebuggerOrFridaPresent() {
        return Debug.isDebuggerConnected() || hasFridaPort();
    }
}
```
```javascript
// Looks correct. Often does nothing.
Java.perform(() => {
    const Checker = Java.use('com.app.Checker');
    Checker.isDebuggerOrFridaPresent.implementation = () => false;
});
```
If the caller and `Checker` are compiled in the same dex and `isDebuggerOrFridaPresent` is small enough, ART's optimizing compiler can fold the entire check into the caller at AOT-compile time on the device (`dex2oat`) or at JIT time. The overwritten `implementation` sits on a method object that the running code no longer calls.
### Forcing the call to exist
Frida's Java bridge exposes a way to tell ART to stop inlining and run everything through the interpreter, where every call is a real call and every hook is reachable:
```javascript
Java.perform(() => {
    Java.deoptimizeEverything(); // interpreter-only, slow, but hooks become reliable
    const Checker = Java.use('com.app.Checker');
    Checker.isDebuggerOrFridaPresent.implementation = () => false;
});
```
`Java.deoptimizeEverything()` is blunt: it disables JIT and treats every method as interpreted for the rest of the process's life, which is slow but removes inlining as a variable while you confirm a hook's logic. `Java.deoptimizeBoundMethod()` narrows the same idea to one already-bound method, at lower cost once you know which call site matters.
### Hooking below the method, not at it
When a target is inlined everywhere it is used, hooking the Java method is the wrong layer. Hooking the native call it eventually reaches (a JNI boundary, a libc function like `ptrace` or `readlink`, or an ART internal such as the interpreter's method-invocation entry point) catches every inlined copy at once, because the native layer those copies all route through was never inlined away.
```javascript
const ptrace = Process.getModuleByName('libc.so').getExportByName('ptrace');
Interceptor.attach(ptrace, {
    onEnter(args) {
        // PTRACE_TRACEME is request 0; a self-trace call is a common
        // debugger/Frida-presence probe implemented in native code.
    },
});
```
## How to recognise it in an authorized lab
1. Hook a method you expect to run, then confirm with a visible side effect (a log line, a thrown exception) that it actually ran at all.
2. If the hook is silent while the app's behaviour still reflects the original logic, suspect inlining before suspecting a typo in the class or method name.
3. Decompile the installed APK (jadx is enough) and check whether the target method is `private`, `final`, `static`, or trivially short — all favour inlining.
4. Re-test with `Java.deoptimizeEverything()` active. If the hook now fires, inlining was the cause.
5. Once confirmed, decide whether to keep deoptimization on (simplest, slowest) or move the hook to a native or framework-level choke point that every inlined copy still passes through.
## Common mistakes and false assumptions
### "The hook installed without an error, so it is active"
Frida's `Java.use(...).method.implementation = fn` succeeds as a JavaScript assignment regardless of whether the runtime ever calls that method object again. A clean script run proves the hook was installed, not that it intercepts anything.
### "Deoptimizing everything is always the fix"
It works, but it is expensive and changes timing-sensitive behaviour. Treat it as a diagnostic step first, and move to a narrower native-layer hook for anything long-running.
### "This only happens with obfuscation"
Inlining is a plain `dex2oat`/JIT optimization. It happens in ordinary release builds with no obfuscator involved, which is why a hook that worked on a debug build can silently stop working on a release one.
## Impact
A defeated hook is invisible by design: the script reports success, the process keeps running, and only the absence of the expected side effect reveals the gap. In an instrumentation-detection gate, this means a player can believe a check is patched while the original, un-hooked logic is still the one deciding the outcome.
## How developers prevent it
Inlining helps attackers avoid detection logic the same way it hides detection logic from legitimate instrumentation, so treat anti-tamper checks as a defense that must not rely on one single call site:
- Duplicate a security-relevant check at more than one layer (Java and native) so defeating one hook point is not sufficient.
- Avoid assuming a single Java-level check is unreachable to native inspection; pair it with native integrity checks that do not depend on a specific compiled call shape.
- Expect that a sufficiently equipped attacker can reach any single in-process check eventually, and do not treat client-side detection as a substitute for server-side verification of anything that grants value.
## Related labs
Apply this technique after studying it:
- [Nexawallet](/labs/nexawallet)
Browse all [labs](/labs), then read [how to play](/play) before starting a lab.
## FAQ
### Does this mean Frida cannot hook final or private methods?
No. Frida can still install the hook. The issue is whether the compiled code still calls that method object at the inlined call site, not whether Frida can reach it.
### Is `Java.deoptimizeEverything()` safe to leave on for a whole engagement?
It is safe but slow, and it changes timing. Use it to confirm a hypothesis, then narrow to a targeted hook once you understand which call site needs it.
### Does this only affect security checks?
No. It affects any Java-layer hook on a method short or final enough to inline, including ordinary logic you are instrumenting for analysis rather than bypass.

## Broken object-level authorization (IDOR)

Source: https://openlabs.duckurity.com/technique/idor

## Overview
Broken object-level authorization is an access-control failure. The application verifies that a request came from a signed-in user, then fails to verify that this user may access the *specific* record named in the request. The older term IDOR, or insecure direct object reference, describes a common way the failure appears.
An object can be an invoice, support case, user profile, document, booking, file, message, or nested resource. The identifier can be a number, UUID, filename, slug, GraphQL variable, or a value hidden in a request body. Its format does not decide security. The server-side authorization check does.
> **Authentication is not authorization**
>
> A valid session proves who sent the request. It does not prove that the sender owns, manages, or may act on the requested object.
OWASP calls this issue [broken object-level authorization](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/). It is part of the broader broken-access-control family.
## Where object references appear
Start by mapping every place where a request selects an object. Do not limit the search to the last number in a URL.
- Path parameters: `GET /api/invoices/inv_1001`
- Query parameters: `GET /api/files?file_id=42`
- JSON bodies: `{"recipient_id":"usr_204"}`
- Form fields and hidden inputs
- GraphQL variables and mutation arguments
- Nested routes: `/teams/team_7/members/usr_204`
- Storage keys, filenames, download tokens, and object URLs
References also occur after an object is created. A client may receive an identifier in a list response, a location header, a link, a browser cache entry, or a WebSocket message. Treat each reference as a request for a server-side permission decision.
## Examples
### Horizontal access failure
Consider a multi-tenant billing product. An ordinary customer can view one of their own invoices:
```http
GET /api/invoices/inv_1001
Authorization: Bearer <customer-session>
```
An unsafe handler fetches the invoice by the client-supplied ID alone:
```python
# Unsafe: the query proves only that the invoice exists.
invoice = invoices.find_one({"id": invoice_id})
return invoice
```
If `inv_1002` belongs to another customer and the same session receives it, the flaw is horizontal privilege escalation. Both users have the same role. One user crossed an ownership boundary.
### Cross-tenant access failure
In a software-as-a-service application, a project manager may be allowed to read every report in their own organisation. A request such as `GET /api/reports/rpt_811` still needs to bind the report to that organisation. A lookup that ignores tenant membership can expose one company to another.
```python
# Safer: retrieve the object inside the authenticated tenant boundary.
report = reports.find_one(
    {"id": report_id, "tenant_id": current_user.tenant_id}
)
if report is None:
    raise HTTPException(status_code=404)
return report
```
The same rule applies to file downloads. A signed URL or opaque storage key should not replace an access decision if the application expects users to have different permissions.
### Write and delete failures
IDOR is not limited to reading data. A customer-service API might correctly show an agent's own drafts but let any authenticated agent update a draft through `PATCH /api/drafts/{id}`. A missing ownership or role check can allow edits, approvals, cancellations, or deletion. Write operations often have a larger business impact than a single data disclosure.
## How to recognise it in an authorized lab
Use accounts and objects that the lab provides. Begin with a normal request. Understand its expected response before changing one object reference.
1. Capture a request for an object that belongs to the current test account.
2. Record the method, object reference, response status, and meaningful fields.
3. Identify a second permitted test object with a different owner, tenant, or role boundary.
4. Change only the object reference. Keep the session and every unrelated field unchanged.
5. Compare the response with the baseline. Check ownership fields and returned content, not only the status code.
6. Repeat separately for read, create, update, and delete flows when the lab exposes them.
A `200 OK` is not proof by itself. The endpoint may return a generic success wrapper, an empty object, or the current user's data. A `403` or `404` can both be valid defensive behaviour. What matters is whether the protected object or action becomes available to the wrong principal.
Use an intercepting proxy, browser developer tools, or a small repeatable HTTP script. Preserve one clean baseline request. It makes comparisons and writeups far more reliable.
## Common mistakes and false assumptions
### "The ID is a UUID, so it is secure"
UUIDs and long random strings make guessing harder. They do not authorize access. IDs leak through lists, links, exports, logs, referrals, browser history, and normal collaboration features. A stolen or discovered UUID still requires an ownership or policy check.
### "The UI hides the button"
The UI is not the security boundary. A route may be hidden from one user while its API still accepts a direct request. Test the request path, not only the screen that generates it.
### "The list endpoint is protected"
Collection and detail endpoints often have different code paths. A filtered list can coexist with an unscoped `GET /resource/{id}`, download, update, or export endpoint.
### "One role check covers every object"
Role-based access control answers broad questions such as whether someone may use a feature. Object-level authorization adds context: which customer's file, which team's project, which user's profile, and which action on it. Many applications need both checks.
## Impact
The impact follows the object and operation. Read access can disclose personal data, financial records, internal files, API keys, or business plans. Write access can alter payment details, permissions, workflow state, or audit records. Cross-tenant exposure can affect every customer of a hosted product.
State the boundary clearly in a report. For example: "an authenticated user in tenant A can read an invoice belonging to tenant B." Avoid vague claims such as "all data is exposed" unless the evidence proves them.
## How developers prevent it
Make authorization part of the object lookup. Query by both the requested ID and the authenticated scope. For more complex policies, use a central authorization service or policy function before returning or changing the object.
- Derive the actor and tenant from the verified session, not from client-controlled fields.
- Apply the check to every method and representation, including downloads, exports, and background jobs.
- Deny by default when an object is missing or outside the allowed scope.
- Test with at least two users and two tenants. Cover read, update, and delete paths.
- Log denied decisions without placing sensitive object contents in logs.
Use opaque identifiers as defense in depth. Do not rely on them as the primary control. [CWE-639](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/639.html) describes the underlying authorization weakness.
## Related labs
Apply this technique after studying it:
- [Duck cross](/labs/duck-cross)
- [Firmdrama](/labs/firmdrama)
Browse all [labs](/labs), then read [how to play](/play) before starting a lab.
## FAQ
### Is IDOR the same as broken access control?
IDOR is a common object-level form of broken access control. Broken access control also includes missing function-level checks and other authorization failures.
### Can a random identifier prevent IDOR?
No. It can reduce casual guessing, but it cannot decide whether the requester may use an identifier they already know.
### Should a secure API return 403 or 404?
Either can be valid. Many APIs return `404` for an inaccessible object to reduce existence disclosure. The important control is that the server does not return or modify an unauthorized object.
### What should I keep in a lab writeup?
Keep the baseline request, the single changed reference, the response evidence, and a concise statement of the crossed authorization boundary.

## Launching an Activity in-process with Frida

Source: https://openlabs.duckurity.com/technique/in-process-activity-launch-with-frida

## Overview
Starting an Activity normally means sending an `Intent` through the Android system, which checks export rules, intent filters, and permissions along the way. Those checks arbitrate access between processes. When Frida is attached to the target app's own process, the same `startActivity()` call can be issued directly from code already running inside that process, which is a different code path from a cross-app launch and is not subject to the same system-level gate.
This page is the practical companion to [non-exported Activity is not an access boundary](/technique/non-exported-activity-is-not-an-access-boundary): that page explains why this works, this page walks through how to do it.
## Examples
### Getting a live Activity reference
The most reliable live `Activity` instance is one the app already created. Hooking a lifecycle method such as `onResume()` on the currently foregrounded Activity captures a real, running instance to act through:
```javascript
Java.perform(() => {
    const Activity = Java.use('android.app.Activity');
    let current = null;
    Activity.onResume.implementation = function () {
        current = this;
        return this.onResume();
    };
    // expose it for the next step once the app is in the foreground
    globalThis.getCurrentActivity = () => current;
});
```
### Building and firing the explicit intent
```javascript
function launchHidden(className) {
    const Intent = Java.use('android.content.Intent');
    const activity = getCurrentActivity();
    if (!activity) {
        console.log('no live Activity yet — bring the app to the foreground first');
        return;
    }
    const pkg = activity.getPackageName();
    const intent = Intent.$new();
    intent.setClassName(pkg, className);
    activity.startActivity(intent);
}
// example:
// launchHidden('com.app.target.AdminPanelActivity');
```
An explicit intent (built with the target class name directly, via `setClassName`) does not need an `<intent-filter>` to resolve, which matters because a hidden Activity usually has none.
### Passing extras the Activity expects
Some hidden Activities branch on an extra that the normal UI would have set before navigating there. Supply it the same way the app would:
```javascript
function launchHiddenWithExtra(className, key, value) {
    const Intent = Java.use('android.content.Intent');
    const activity = getCurrentActivity();
    const intent = Intent.$new();
    intent.setClassName(activity.getPackageName(), className);
    intent.putExtra(key, value);
    activity.startActivity(intent);
}
```
Read the target Activity's `onCreate()`/`getIntent()` calls in a decompile first to know which extras it reads and what it does when one is missing, rather than guessing.
## How to recognise it in an authorized lab
1. Confirm from the decompiled manifest which Activities exist and are not reachable through the app's normal navigation.
2. Attach Frida to the running app (spawn-gate with `-f` for full control from process start, or attach to an already-running instance).
3. Capture a live `Activity` reference through a lifecycle hook, since `startActivity()` is an instance method that needs a `Context`.
4. Build an explicit `Intent` naming the target class and fire it through the live `Activity`'s `startActivity()`.
5. Supply any extras the target Activity's `onCreate()` expects, discovered by reading the decompiled code rather than trial and error.
6. Observe what the Activity does once reached, and note separately whether reaching it required defeating any other check (for example, an instrumentation-detection gate) first.
## Common mistakes and false assumptions
### "This needs the app's own source code"
It needs the class name and package name, both readable from a decompiled APK, and knowledge of expected extras from reading `onCreate()`. No source access or rebuild is required.
### "An implicit intent will also work"
Usually not, because a non-exported Activity commonly has no `<intent-filter>` for the system to match against. An explicit intent built with `setClassName()` bypasses filter resolution entirely and is the reliable approach here.
### "You need a currently visible Activity of the exact right type"
Any live `Activity` instance in the target process works as the `Context` for `startActivity()`. It does not need to be related to the target Activity; it only needs to exist and be attached to a running window so the system accepts the call.
## Impact
This is the mechanism, not the finding. The actual severity depends on what the reached Activity does: a benign debug screen is low impact, while an Activity that mints a privileged token, approves a transaction, or exposes data meant to be access-controlled is high impact, because it is reachable without going through whatever checks the normal UI flow enforces first.
## How developers prevent it
- Do not rely on reachability (export status) as the only gate on a sensitive Activity; verify authorization inside it, ideally against server-held state.
- Treat any Activity's `onCreate()` as attacker-reachable code once the app can be instrumented, and validate extras defensively rather than trusting that only the app's own UI supplies them.
- Where possible, require a fresh server round-trip to authorize the action the Activity performs, so reaching the screen does not itself grant the capability.
## Related labs
Apply this technique after studying it:
- [Nexawallet](/labs/nexawallet)
Browse all [labs](/labs), then read [how to play](/play) before starting a lab.
## FAQ
### Does this require root or a jailbroken-style environment?
No. It requires an emulator or device where Frida can attach to the target process, which on a standard development/test emulator does not require root.
### Is this specific to Frida, or does the underlying issue apply more broadly?
The underlying issue (non-export is not an in-process boundary) applies to any tooling that can execute code in the target process. Frida is the common practical tool for doing so during an authorized assessment.
### What stops this from working on every app?
Nothing about `startActivity()` itself. What varies is what the reached Activity requires to do anything useful (extras, prior app state) and whether other in-process defenses, such as instrumentation detection, must be defeated first to get a stable attach.

## Mass assignment

Source: https://openlabs.duckurity.com/technique/mass-assignment

## Overview
Mass assignment happens when a server takes a client-controlled object and automatically copies its properties onto an internal model. It is also called auto-binding or over-posting. The convenience becomes dangerous when the model contains properties that the client must not set.
For example, a profile form may only let a user change their display name and time zone. The underlying account record may also contain `is_staff`, `account_tier`, `owner_id`, `credit_limit`, or `email_verified`. If the update endpoint accepts the entire record, an added property can reach the database even though the UI never exposes it.
OWASP groups these failures under [broken object property level authorization](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa3-broken-object-property-level-authorization/). Mass assignment describes the unsafe binding mechanism that often enables them.
> **The request body is the trust boundary**
>
> The fields shown by a form are not an allowlist. A client can send any valid JSON property, including one that the front end never renders.
## Why it happens
Frameworks make it easy to deserialize JSON into an object, merge a patch into a model, or map fields onto an ORM record. That is useful for public fields. It is unsafe when the same model also contains permissions, ownership, approval state, financial limits, or internal workflow flags.
Risk grows when an API does any of the following:
- Binds an entire request object directly to a database entity.
- Uses a generic `update`, `merge`, or `setattr` loop.
- Reuses one schema for API input, API output, and storage.
- Supports `PATCH`, JSON Patch, GraphQL mutations, or bulk-edit features without per-field policy checks.
- Returns sensitive fields in a response and accepts the same shape on update.
## Examples
### A profile update that trusts every field
Imagine a customer portal that accepts this normal request:
```http
PATCH /api/profile
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "display_name": "Nora",
  "time_zone": "Africa/Cairo"
}
```
An unsafe handler loops through every submitted property:
```python
# Unsafe: each client-supplied name becomes a model update.
for name, value in request.json.items():
    setattr(account, name, value)
database.save(account)
```
The issue is not the visible fields. It is the absence of a server-side list of properties this actor may change. A production-style test might add one suspected protected field to an otherwise valid request and then verify whether the server persisted it on the current test account.
### A registration flow that sets account state
Registration endpoints can have the same flaw. A service may legitimately accept `name`, `email`, and `password`, while the stored object also includes `plan`, `is_partner`, and `approval_status`. If registration binds the full object, a new account can be created with an unintended state.
### A generic patch endpoint
JSON Patch makes each property explicit, but it does not enforce policy on its own:
```json
[
  {"op": "replace", "path": "/display_name", "value": "Nora"},
  {"op": "replace", "path": "/account_tier", "value": "enterprise"}
]
```
The API must validate every patch path and every requested value. Checking only that the JSON is well formed leaves protected properties reachable.
## How to recognise it in an authorized lab
Start with a normal create or update request. Establish which fields are intended to be editable for the current account.
1. Save a clean baseline request and the resulting object state.
2. Compare the UI fields, API documentation, request body, and response body.
3. List fields that look server-owned, role-related, financial, approval-related, or ownership-related.
4. Add one candidate property to the original valid request. Do not change unrelated fields.
5. Fetch the current test object's state again and compare the specific property.
6. Record whether the property was rejected, ignored, normalized, or persisted.
Test one property at a time. An error may mean a validation rule worked, a type was wrong, or the field was not recognised. A successful HTTP status can also mean the field was silently ignored. Verify the saved state through an allowed response or action.
Useful places to inspect include account settings, invitations, checkout flows, bulk editors, support tickets, content-management forms, and GraphQL mutations. Look for fields that exist in responses but not in the normal form. Treat them as hypotheses, not proof.
## What mass assignment is not
### It is not only an admin flag
Changing `is_admin` is an obvious example, but protected fields can also control ownership, spending limits, verification, discounts, approval status, feature access, or workflow state. A property can be security-sensitive without having an alarming name.
### It is not the same as IDOR
IDOR asks whether the requester may act on a particular object. Mass assignment asks whether the requester may change a particular property. One endpoint can have both problems. A secure design checks object ownership and limits writable properties.
### It is not proven by an echoed response
Some APIs reflect unrecognized properties in a temporary response. Others serialize calculated fields that cannot be written. Prove a finding by observing persistent server-side state or a meaningful server-controlled behaviour change in the lab.
## Impact
The impact depends on the property. A changed marketing preference may have little effect. A changed role, owner, approval state, or payment limit can undermine an entire business process. Automatic binding can also expose data on reads when an API returns properties that were meant to stay internal.
Describe the impact as a specific unauthorized state transition. For example: "a standard account can set a server-managed approval state on its own profile." That is stronger and more useful than saying that arbitrary fields are accepted.
## How developers prevent it
Use dedicated input schemas. Define the few fields that an endpoint accepts, then construct the update explicitly. Keep permissions and server-managed state outside the client-controlled update object.
```python
# Safer: the endpoint chooses each permitted field.
changes = {
    "display_name": body.display_name,
    "time_zone": body.time_zone,
}
account.update(changes)
database.save(account)
```
- Allowlist writable fields for each endpoint and role.
- Use separate request, response, and persistence models.
- Reject unknown properties where the framework permits it.
- Validate JSON Patch paths and GraphQL mutation arguments explicitly.
- Derive ownership, roles, prices, and approvals on the server.
- Add negative tests for every protected property and sensitive state transition.
[CWE-915](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/915.html) covers this class as improperly controlled modification of dynamically determined object attributes.
## Related labs
Apply this technique after studying it:
- [Firmdrama](/labs/firmdrama)
Browse all [labs](/labs), then read [how to play](/play) before starting a lab.
## FAQ
### Is mass assignment the same as broken object property level authorization?
Mass assignment is a common way an API permits an unauthorized property change. Broken object property level authorization is the broader outcome: the API fails to enforce who may read or modify a sensitive property.
### Does hiding a field in the UI fix it?
No. The server must reject or ignore the field. A client can edit a request outside the UI.
### What is the safest first test?
Use your own authorized test object, preserve a normal request, add one low-impact candidate property, and verify the stored result. Do not send broad property lists.
### Can PATCH be secure?
Yes. PATCH is safe when the server allowlists paths and applies authorization and validation to every supported property.

## A non-exported Activity is not an access boundary

Source: https://openlabs.duckurity.com/technique/non-exported-activity-is-not-an-access-boundary

## Overview
`android:exported="false"` on an `<activity>` tells the Android package manager to refuse an intent that originates from another application's process. It is an inter-process access control, enforced at the point where the system would otherwise hand a cross-app Intent to your component. It says nothing about code that is already running inside your own process.
Treating a non-exported Activity as hidden from the player misreads what the flag protects. A debugger, a Frida agent, or any native code attached to the running app's own process is not "another app" from the system's point of view. It is the app. Code with that vantage point can call `startActivity()` the same way the app's own code would, because it is making the call from inside the same process the Activity belongs to.
> **Process boundary, not code boundary**
>
> `exported="false"` stops Android's inter-process intent-resolution path. It does not create a privilege boundary between different pieces of code sharing one process.
## Examples
### What `exported="false"` actually stops
```xml
<activity
    android:name=".AdminPanelActivity"
    android:exported="false" />
```
Another installed app sending an explicit intent for `AdminPanelActivity` is rejected by the system before the component ever starts:
```java
// From a different app's process — refused by the OS.
Intent i = new Intent();
i.setClassName("com.app.target", "com.app.target.AdminPanelActivity");
startActivity(i); // SecurityException: not exported
```
### What it does not stop
From inside the target app's own process — which is exactly where an attached Frida agent executes — the same call succeeds, because the system sees it as the app launching its own component:
```javascript
Java.perform(() => {
    const Activity = Java.use('android.app.Activity');
    const Intent = Java.use('android.content.Intent');
    const currentActivity = /* obtain a live Activity instance, e.g. via Activity.onResume hook */;
    const intent = Intent.$new();
    intent.setClassName('com.app.target', 'com.app.target.AdminPanelActivity');
    currentActivity.startActivity(intent);
});
```
No manifest check runs here that would reject an in-process caller, because the manifest-level export check exists to arbitrate between processes, and this call never crosses a process boundary.
## How to recognise it in an authorized lab
1. Decompile the APK and list every `<activity>` with `android:exported="false"` or no `android:exported` attribute at all (the default depends on whether the Activity declares an intent-filter).
2. Check whether the hidden Activity's `onCreate()` performs the sensitive action directly, or only after further checks (a PIN, a role flag, a server round-trip). The export flag alone tells you reachability, not what happens once reached.
3. From an attached Frida session in the target process, obtain a live `Activity`, `Context`, or `Application` reference and issue an explicit intent naming the hidden Activity's class.
4. Confirm the Activity starts and observe what it exposes once reached — note that reaching it is a separate finding from any further logic flaw inside it.
## Common mistakes and false assumptions
### "It's not exported, so it's not reachable"
Exported controls who outside the app can start it. It does not hide the component from code already running inside the app's own process, including instrumentation attached to that process.
### "Hiding the entry point is a mitigation"
An unreachable-from-outside Activity still ships inside the APK and still runs with the app's full in-process privileges once reached. It reduces the number of ways in, not the value of reaching it.
### "This requires root"
It does not. It requires the ability to attach to the target process (Frida's `-f`/spawn-gate or an attach to a debuggable or otherwise instrumentable process), which on a development or test device does not require root.
## Impact
Any sensitive action gated purely by non-export status — an admin panel, a debug menu, a privileged settings screen, a flag-granting state — is reachable by anything that can execute in the app's own process. The severity depends on what the Activity does once started, not on whether it was reachable from another app.
## How developers prevent it
- Treat `exported="false"` as process isolation, never as a user- or capability-level permission boundary.
- Gate sensitive actions by server-verified state, not by which component the client happened to launch.
- If an in-app debug or admin surface must exist, remove it from release builds entirely rather than relying on it being merely non-exported.
- Pair any in-process-reachable sensitive action with its own authorization check that does not assume only the "front door" (the exported entry point) leads to it.
## Related labs
Apply this technique after studying it:
- [Nexawallet](/labs/nexawallet)
Browse all [labs](/labs), then read [how to play](/play) before starting a lab.
## FAQ
### Does setting exported to false do anything useful at all?
Yes. It correctly blocks other installed apps from launching the component via an intent, which matters for components that should only ever be reached from inside your own app's normal navigation flow.
### Is this the same issue as an insecure deep link?
They are related but distinct. A deep link issue is usually about an *exported* component accepting unsafe input from outside. This technique is about a *non-exported* component being reachable from inside the same process regardless of export status.
### Does enabling `android:permission` on the Activity fix this?
A custom permission still gates the inter-process path the same way export does. It does not add a check against code already running in-process, since in-process calls never go through the permission-checked IPC path.

## SQL injection

Source: https://openlabs.duckurity.com/technique/sqli

## Overview
SQL injection occurs when untrusted input is incorporated into a database query without appropriate parameterization or validation. Player-controlled input can alter the intended SQL query and may expose records beyond the application's normal search behavior.
## Examples
See the [duckrpc-archive](/labs/duckrpc-archive) lab for a gRPC archive service that mishandles query input.
## Related labs
- [duckrpc-archive](/labs/duckrpc-archive)
Browse all [labs](/labs) when it is solved.
## FAQ
### Is every SQL error a SQL injection?
No. An error may only mean the query failed. Injection requires proof that attacker-controlled input changed query behavior.
Read [how to play](/play) for the usual solve loop.

## Server-side request forgery (SSRF)

Source: https://openlabs.duckurity.com/technique/ssrf

## Overview
SSRF happens when a server-side feature fetches a URL that you supply, and that server has network access you don't. Point it at an internal hostname or port and the response comes back through the feature that was only meant to fetch public resources.
## Examples
Watch for any field that fetches a resource by URL: image imports, webhook URLs, PDF generators, link previews. Try internal hostnames, `localhost`, alternate ports, and cloud metadata addresses. Compare response timing and content for signs the request actually reached an internal target.
## Related labs
Practise on a live target:
- [TechVault](/labs/techvault) — an internal service reachable only through a chained request.
Browse all [labs](/labs) when it is solved.
## FAQ
**Is SSRF only useful for reading internal web pages?**
No. It's often a stepping stone — reaching an internal API, metadata endpoint, or service that then exposes a further flaw.
**Do I need special tooling?**
A browser or `curl` is enough to start. Read [how to play](/play) for the loop.

## Server-side template injection (SSTI)

Source: https://openlabs.duckurity.com/technique/ssti

## Overview
Server-side template injection happens when an application treats user input as template *source* instead of template *data*. Template engines turn a fixed template and a data context into HTML, email, a PDF, a report, or another response. If a user-controlled value becomes part of the template source before rendering, the engine can evaluate template syntax inside that value.
This is different from simply showing submitted text in a page. A safe application keeps its template fixed and passes untrusted text as a value. An unsafe application builds a new template string from that text and then asks the engine to execute it.
> **Escaping is not the primary fix**
>
> HTML escaping protects the output context. It does not make it safe to compile untrusted text as a server-side template. Keep template source fixed.
## Why template engines are sensitive
Template languages provide expressions, variables, loops, conditions, filters, and helper functions. Those features are useful to developers. Once untrusted input reaches the template compiler, the same features can expose data from the rendering context or invoke behaviour the author never intended.
Potential impact depends on the engine, configuration, available context, and host privileges. A finding might only alter rendered content. It can also disclose server-side values, access files, make internal requests, or lead to server-side code execution in a weakly isolated environment. Do not assume the maximum impact without evidence.
## Examples
### A support-email preview
Imagine a support tool that previews a customer message before sending it. The unsafe implementation builds template source through string concatenation:
```python
# Unsafe: message becomes part of the Jinja source code.
source = "<h1>Support reply</h1><p>" + message + "</p>"
html = render_template_string(source)
```
The safe implementation keeps the page structure in a reviewed template file and supplies `message` as data:
```python
# Safer: preview.html is fixed template source.
html = render_template("preview.html", message=message)
```
Inside `preview.html`, the developer renders `{{ message }}`. The syntax belongs to the trusted template, not to the submitted message.
### A report generator
Report, invoice, and PDF features often combine user labels with a template engine. A service that formats a title with a language-level string interpolation and then compiles the result as a template creates the same risk. The correct design passes the title, recipient, and report data as named variables to a fixed template.
### A user-selectable template
Some products let administrators choose from several approved email layouts. That can be safe when the server maps a short key such as `"receipt"` to an allowlisted template file. It becomes risky when a client can submit raw template text or influence a template path without strict validation. Template-path traversal is a separate issue, but both flaws come from treating template selection as untrusted input.
## How to recognise it in an authorized lab
Look for endpoints that render or preview text. Common candidates include emails, notifications, invoices, document generators, report builders, CMS previews, localization features, and printable receipts.
1. Submit a harmless literal marker and find where it appears in the response.
2. Use error messages, documentation, response conventions, or client code to form a hypothesis about the template engine.
3. Submit one harmless arithmetic expression that matches the suspected syntax, such as `{{ 7 * 7 }}` for Jinja-style engines.
4. Compare the rendered output with the literal baseline. A computed result is evidence that the input reached an expression evaluator.
5. Confirm the rendering context and input field with a minimal, repeatable request.
6. Stop at the evidence needed by the lab. Avoid destructive payloads, resource-intensive expressions, and changes outside the authorized target.
A result such as `49` is a strong signal only when the application returns the rendered server response. A client-side script, a calculation feature, or a different transformation can create misleading output. Capture the request and response. Record why the behaviour indicates server-side template evaluation.
## Template syntax is engine-specific
Do not use one syntax everywhere. Template languages differ.
| Family | Common expression form | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Jinja and Twig | `{{ 7 * 7 }}` | Python and PHP applications |
| FreeMarker | `${7 * 7}` | Java applications |
| EJS | `<%= 7 * 7 %>` | Node.js applications |
The table is a starting point, not an engine fingerprint. Syntax can be customized, expressions can be disabled, and errors can be hidden. Choose a benign probe only after gathering evidence. Never treat an error string as a full map of the server environment.
## SSTI, XSS, and similar issues
### SSTI versus XSS
Cross-site scripting runs in a visitor's browser. SSTI runs while the server renders a template. XSS defenses such as Content Security Policy and HTML output encoding do not replace a server-side template-source boundary.
### SSTI versus expression injection
Some products evaluate expressions in spreadsheets, search filters, workflow rules, or client-side frameworks. The testing method can look similar. Identify the interpreter and where it runs before classifying the issue.
### Reflected text is not enough
If a submitted string appears in a response unchanged, it may simply be normal reflection. The key evidence is that the server interpreted template syntax contained in the input.
## How developers prevent it
Use static templates stored with the application. Pass user-controlled values as data to the renderer. Keep template selection to a server-side allowlist. Do not use concatenation, runtime compilation, or a dynamic-template API with untrusted text.
- Separate template source, template selection, and template data.
- Enable output encoding for the target format, such as HTML, even after fixing SSTI.
- Keep the rendering process low-privilege and restrict its access to secrets and local files.
- Treat user-authored templates as a high-risk product feature. Isolate and sandbox them rather than mixing them with application templates.
- Add tests that submit template delimiters as ordinary user data and assert that they remain literal.
- Review email, PDF, preview, export, and notification paths during code review.
## Related labs
Apply this technique after studying it:
- [Firmdrama](/labs/firmdrama)
Browse all [labs](/labs), then read [how to play](/play) before starting a lab.
## FAQ
### Is SSTI always remote code execution?
No. The result depends on the engine, available objects, sandboxing, and process privileges. A safe report describes the behaviour that was actually proven.
### Does autoescaping prevent SSTI?
No. Autoescaping protects how a value is placed into output. SSTI begins earlier, when the value is made part of template source.
### Why use arithmetic as a first test?
It is a small, non-destructive way to distinguish literal rendering from expression evaluation when the syntax matches the suspected engine.
### What should I include in a lab writeup?
Include the benign baseline, the minimal expression, the rendered result, the likely engine evidence, and the security boundary that the server crossed.
